title: How Scabies Work
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss scabies, the itch caused by the mite Sarcoptes scabiei: how the female burrows into skin and lays eggs, transmission through prolonged close contact (including sexual contact, shared beds and towels), symptoms such as nighttime itching and rashes, common body locations in adults and children, crusted (Norwegian) scabies, treatment with prescription permethrin (Elimite) and lindane (Lindane) scabicides, itch relief with calamine and cool baths, washing clothes and bedding, and home remedies like neem and tea tree oil and sulfur ointment. They also cover chiggers (not burrowing), myths about scabies and hygiene, and a listener email about Braille on currency and grade one versus grade two Braille. Includes intro banter about Chuck's illness and Guatemala trip, and Amish/Walmart listener mail.

segments.title: Opening banter and Guatemala trip
segments.summary: Chuck has been unwell after returning from Guatemala; hosts joke about Montezuma's revenge and ice in drinks. Josh introduces scabies as the topic, prompted by a friend's case.

segments.title: How scabies spreads and the burrowing mite
segments.summary: Scabies affects about 300 million people a year. The female mite burrows into skin and lays eggs, which mature within about fourteen days, so one mite can start an infestation. Symptoms can take weeks to months to appear, while the person is already contagious. Spread occurs through prolonged close contact, including sexual contact, sharing beds, towels and clothing. Soap and water do not remove mites under the skin.

segments.title: Symptoms, locations and crusted scabies
segments.summary: Symptoms include intense itching, worse at night, a reddish bumpy rash, and sometimes burrow trails. The itch is an allergic reaction to mites and their feces. Common adult sites include wrists, elbows, armpits, waist, buttocks, between fingers, penis and nipples; children are affected on the scalp, face, neck and palms. Crusted (Norwegian) scabies involves thick crusts with millions of mites, is highly contagious, and often causes less itching, sometimes in people who cannot scratch.

segments.title: Scabies treatment and prevention
segments.summary: A doctor will usually prescribe a topical scabicide such as permethrin (Elimite) or lindane, left on for hours and washed off, usually effective after one treatment. Itching may persist for weeks. Calamine and cool baths relieve itch but do not kill mites. Family members should be treated too, and clothing and bedding washed on hot or sanitize settings or dry cleaned.

segments.title: Home remedies, chiggers and scabies myths
segments.summary: Neem paste and diluted tea tree oil are mentioned as home options; a study found sulfur ointment as effective as prescribed ointments for children. Myths covered: scabies does not strike all races equally, chiggers do not burrow (they feed on top of skin), scabies does not mean a person is dirty or promiscuous.

segments.title: Listener mail: Amish and Walmart; Braille on currency
segments.summary: Hosts respond to listener emails about Amish shoppers at Walmart. A listener from Ottawa, Ontario, who is blind, explains that grade two Braille is common in public places, grade one is useful for spelling, and Canadian bills have Braille cells that fade over time.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener emails and close the episode.
